title: Eye Clinic Language Access: A Clinical Workflow
summary: Build an eye-clinic language access workflow for scheduling, testing, imaging, dilation, eye-drop teach-back, checkout, and follow-up.
body_markdown:
###


Interpretation should start at the first clinically meaningful exchange, which may occur during scheduling, symptom triage, check-in, or technician history. In an eye clinic, waiting until the ophthalmologist enters can leave testing instructions, medication reconciliation, and urgent symptom questions without adequate language support.


###


The clinic should assign ownership at each handoff, keep the approved device with the patient when practical, and confirm the language, dialect, and active method after every move. If a session disconnects, staff should reconnect or use the documented backup before continuing imaging, dilation, examination, or counseling.


###


The clinician should state the medication, eye, number of drops, frequency, duration, and taper in short segments, then ask the patient or caregiver to explain and demonstrate the plan. National Eye Institute guidance says to wait at least five minutes between different types of eye drops and to follow the prescribed instructions.


###


No. Spoken interpretation supports the live conversation, while written translation converts documents such as preparation instructions, medication schedules, and after-visit summaries. Eye clinics should coordinate both and use teach-back because a translated document by itself does not confirm understanding.


###


An eye clinic should use or switch to a qualified human interpreter when the patient prefers one, audio or privacy is inadequate, the language or dialect is not supported, uncertainty persists after clarification, the technology fails, or organizational policy calls for escalation. The choice should reflect the patient, setting, and communication task.
